title: Can Your CRM Handle Customer Success?
summary: Can your CRM handle customer success? See when a CRM is enough and how Outlit covers accounts teams cannot review by hand.
body_markdown:
## TL;dr


Can your CRM handle customer success? It can while the record still tells an owner what changed and what to do next. Once people rebuild that story by hand, the CRM vs customer success platform question is real. A customer success platform (CSP) helps a team run its post-sale work. Outlit fits when the team can't review every account and investigates changes by hand: it monitors connected sources, starts investigations when something changes, and proposes customer work a person approves.


## When is the CRM enough?


If you have a few dozen accounts, owners know their customers by name, and renewals turn mostly on the relationship, a disciplined CRM with a handful of lifecycle stages will carry you. A second system means another login and another place for data to drift. Stages nobody updates, owners who left, and blank renewal dates are cheaper to fix than to replace, and you'll need them fixed either way.


The CRM stops being enough when the record no longer holds the story. Take an illustrative account. The renewal is 60 days out and the CRM says on track because the last call went well. Since then, weekly active users dropped in PostHog, a migration ticket in Pylon reopened twice, and the champion asked about export options in Gmail. The CRM isn't wrong. It's three weeks behind. Synced properties and workflows can flag the usage drop and the ticket. Connecting them to the export question and deciding what to do is still left to someone.


## When does a customer success platform earn its seat?


When the problem is running the post-sale work, not recording the deal. Each CSM keeps a private spreadsheet, onboarding depends on who ran it, and a manager can't say which accounts had a business review last quarter without asking around. A CSP gives the team one place where each account's state and plan live, and that's worth paying for.


CSPs differ on what happens next. Some center on health scores and playbooks. Others add agents that investigate and propose work. On the 60-day account, a health score might drop and a task might open, leaving a CSM to work out whether the drop is a real problem, a holiday week, or a champion who changed roles. Some products go further. Running the account through each one shows which kind you're looking at.


## How do you test a setup on one account?


Run one of your own accounts through the CRM, each CSP on the shortlist, and Outlit, and ask:


- What started the work: a person's question, a scheduled review, or a change in the data?
- What did it read, and can you open the source behind each claim?
- What does it say it doesn't know?
- What work did it propose, did that build on what the owner already agreed, and who approves it?
- After the work is done, does it keep checking whether the risk went away?


Whatever a system doesn't produce is work your people are still doing.


### Evidence check


For the 60-day account, a useful answer looks something like this. It's illustrative.


- **What changed:** weekly active users fell for three weeks after a good call, the migration ticket reopened twice, and the champion asked about export options.
- **Sources and dates:**` PostHog` usage since the call on` day -21` ;` Pylon` ticket reopened on` day -14` and` day -6` ;` Gmail` note on` day -3` ;` HubSpot` stage unchanged since the call.
- **What tempers it:** a customer mid-migration asks about exports too. The note alone doesn't show intent to leave.
- **Decision:** the owner asks the champion whether the migration blocker is behind the export question, before any renewal conversation.
- **Next check:** whether the ticket closes and usage recovers within two weeks of the reply.


## When should you use Outlit?


Outlit runs next to the CRM, which stays the commercial record. It fits when:


- your team can't routinely review every account
- people assemble and investigate changing account evidence by hand
- findings need to become work done with customers


Outlit is proactive. It monitors connected sources and starts an investigation when something changes, such as falling usage, a spike in support tickets, an escalation, or a billing problem, without waiting for someone to ask or for a scheduled review. On the 60-day account, it weighs the usage drop, the reopened ticket, and the export question against the account's history, says which evidence is missing, and links each claim to its[source](https://docs.outlit.ai/concepts/customer-context-graph) where one exists.


It then proposes specific steps, informed by what was already promised, such as a drafted email asking the champion whether the migration blocker explains the export question. A person decides which steps to take, and reviews and sends each email through their connected Gmail account. Finishing the work doesn't close the risk. The assessment stays open until the evidence changes.


## What should happen when the systems disagree?


Disagreement is normal, and it's usually the most informative thing on the account. HubSpot is right about who owns it and when it renews. Stripe is right that the invoice was paid. PostHog is right that usage halved. The mistake is letting one stand in for the others, so a paid invoice becomes renewal intent or a closed ticket becomes a solved problem. A good setup keeps each fact tied to its source and the conflict visible to the reviewer, not blended into a score. That's the job of the[customer context infrastructure](https://www.outlit.ai/blog/what-is-customer-context-infrastructure) underneath Outlit's agents.


## Which should you add first?


If commercial records are unreliable, fix the CRM before buying anything. If the post-sale work needs a system of its own, shop for a CSP. If accounts change faster than your team can check them, look at Outlit. Run the same account test on each. Start with[how Outlit protects and grows long-tail revenue](https://www.outlit.ai/) , then read[how Outlit works a renewal](https://www.outlit.ai/blog/how-to-run-your-renewal-process-with-outlit) , which follows one account as its blocker changes.
